Commander
kŏm-mănd´ĕr
n. (one who gives orders; a messianic title in Isaiah's great invitation)
From Latin commendare, to entrust, and mandare, to command. Isaiah 55:4 renders Hebrew metsavveh, one who gives charge — the participle of the verb behind mitzvah, commandment.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah's open invitation is not to a philosophy but to a Person with authority: “Behold, I have given him for a witness to the people, a leader and commander to the people” (Isaiah 55:4). Three titles in one line, and the third is military. He testifies, He goes in front, and He gives orders. The chapter has already set the terms of the covenant He heads: “Incline your ear, and come unto me: hear, and your soul shall live; and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David” (Isaiah 55:3) — a covenant whose mercies are sure because they rest on David's greater Son and not on the comers. And the invitation itself is free to the penniless: “Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price” (Isaiah 55:1). Isaiah had already named the child on whose shoulder the government would rest: “For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6). Grace is free, and the One who gives it is a Commander. Both stand in the same chapter.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a commander as a chief; one who has supreme authority; a leader; the chief officer of an army, or of any division of it.

expand to see more

COMMANDER, n. A chief; one who has supreme authority; a leader; the chief officer of an army, or of any division of it.

COMMANDER, n. One who has supreme authority over a ship or fleet; a commanding officer.

COMMAND, v.t. [L. mando, to command, to commit.] To bid; to order; to direct; to charge; implying authority, and power to control, and to require obedience.

LEADER, n. One that leads or conducts; a guide; a conductor; a chief; a commander.

WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event. That which furnishes evidence or proof.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 55:4 — "Behold, I have given him for a witness to the people, a leader and commander to the people."

Isaiah 55:3 — "Incline your ear, and come unto me: hear, and your soul shall live; and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David."

Isaiah 55:1 — "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price."

Isaiah 9:6 — "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace."

Modern Corruption

The invitation of Isaiah 55 is preached without verse 4, so that Christ is offered as a Saviour to be received and not as a Commander to be obeyed.

expand to see more

Isaiah 55:1 is one of the freest offers in Scripture — no money, no price, come and buy. Three verses later the same chapter names the One offered as a leader and commander. The gospel that keeps verse 1 and drops verse 4 produces a convert who has received a benefit and acknowledged no authority, and Scripture knows no such creature. The 1689 confesses that saving faith receives Christ as prophet, priest, and king; a faith that takes the priest and declines the king has divided a Person who cannot be divided.

The opposite error deserves naming in the same breath, because the remedy for cheap grace is not a price tag. Verse 1 is addressed to the man who hath no money, and every attempt to add a qualification — sufficient sorrow, a settled life, a demonstrated seriousness — contradicts the verse it claims to guard. The mercies are called sure in verse 3 precisely because they do not rest on the comer. Free to enter, and a Commander inside: that is the whole chapter, and neither half may be preached alone.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew metsavveh (H6680), one commanding, from tsavah, to give charge; nagid (H5057), leader, prince; ed (H5707), a witness.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsavah (H6680) — to lay charge upon, command; its participle gives commander.

Hebrew nagid (H5057) — leader, prince, one set in front; the second title of Isaiah 55:4.

Hebrew ed (H5707) — a witness; the first title, one who testifies.

Hebrew chesed Dawid ha-neemanim (H2617) — the sure mercies of David; quoted in Acts 13:34.

Hebrew misrah (H4951) — government, rule; Isaiah 9:6, upon his shoulder.

Usage

"“A leader and commander to the people” — three titles, and one gives orders."

"“He that hath no money” — the qualification is that there is none."

"“The sure mercies of David” — sure because they do not rest on the comer."
